 Losing sleep could make you an easier target for cybercriminals
 University of California researchers say even a small disruption to sleep could affect decision-making, making people less likely to spot fraudulent emails.
 Romal Renny

 New Delhi : Losing even a small amount of sleep could make people more vulnerable to online scams, according to a new study that found employees were 13% more likely to click suspicious email links following the annual transition to daylight saving time in the United States.
 Published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences on 11 November, the study examined the responses of 11,218 employees at the University of California, Irvine, to simulated phishing emails sent before and after the clocks moved forward by an hour in March 2026.
 Phishing involves sending fraudulent messages that appear legitimate to trick recipients into revealing sensitive information or visiting malicious websites.
 Show Full Article
 How sleep loss affects decision-making 
 Eitan Schechtman, a neurobiology researcher at UC Irvine, conducted the experiment using the university’s existing cybersecurity awareness programme, which periodically sends simulated phishing emails to employees.
 “I was wondering, as a sleep researcher, what sleep would do to that,” Schechtman told TIME .
 The researchers randomly assigned 5,620 employees to receive a simulated phishing email on 2 March, before the daylight saving transition, while another 5,598 received the same email on 9 March, immediately after the clocks changed.
 Among those who received the email before the transition, 15.66% clicked the suspicious link, compared with 17.76 per cent afterwards. The study found no significant differences in how frequently employees opened the emails or reported them as spam.
 Schechtman suggested that sleep deprivation made employees more impulsive and less likely to scrutinise suspicious messages before clicking links. The difference was particularly noticeable immediately after the emails were delivered, peaking around 70 seconds after their arrival.
 “Our interpretation of this is that sleep loss rendered people more impulsive and less likely to carefully think about their decisions, so they open the email and they’re like, ‘OK, here’s this link. I’ll just click it.’” Schechtman recalls. “They didn’t have their full mental capacity to critically examine whether this might be an email that’s trying to lead them astray.”

 Implications for cybersecurity 
 Jason RC Nurse, a cybersecurity researcher at the University of Kent who was not involved in the study, told TIME that sleep deprivation could impair people’s ability to assess suspicious messages:
 “Sleep deprivation can fit this profile in some ways,” he remarked, “If we’re not thinking properly or rationally about what we’re seeing in our inboxes, there’s every chance that we might get caught out and fall for a phishing attempt.”
 However, the study did not directly measure how much sleep individual employees lost. The daylight saving transition also changes light exposure and disrupts the body’s internal clock, meaning the researchers could not isolate sleep deprivation as the sole explanation.
 Despite the relatively light-hearted nature of this study, there have been more serious studies that link sleep deprivation to more dangerous acts of carelessness such as fatal car crashes .
 Schechtman has since collected additional data from the November transition back to standard time, although these findings have yet to be analysed. He hopes other institutions will replicate the experiment to establish whether the findings apply more broadly.
 (Edited by Janaki Pande)
